extracted.intended_audience: employers, workers, labor lawyers, human resources/compliance officers, and Department of Labor investigators
extracted.subtask_description: Final rule text from the Department of Labor setting forth the economic reality test and related regulatory guidance for determining whether a worker is an employee or an independent contractor under the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA). It explains the factors to consider, accompanying examples, and how to weigh relevant facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic dependence (ultimate inquiry)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate inquiry is whether, as a matter of economic reality, the worker is economically dependent on the employer for work (and thus an employee) or is in business for themself (and thus an independent contractor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The economic reality test's purpose is to assess economic dependence; independent contractors are workers who are not economically dependent on an employer and are in business for themselves. This framing guides application of all factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality-of-the-circumstances analysis / No predetermined weight for factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine status using a totality-of-the-circumstances economic reality test in which the factors do not have predetermined weight and no one factor or subset of factors is necessarily dispositive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the economic realities of the whole activity; consider all relevant factors together rather than elevating or rigidly prioritizing any factor(s). This returns to longstanding judicial and Department practice and departs from any approach assigning fixed weights ('core' vs 'non-core').

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity for profit or loss depending on managerial skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the worker has an opportunity for profit or risk of loss that depends on their managerial skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the worker can affect their earnings through managerial decisions (e.g., ability to increase revenue or control costs); this factor looks to entrepreneurial opportunities rather than mere variations in hours or productivity. Examples in the rule illustrate application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investments by the worker and the potential employer
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the investments made by the worker and by the potential employer (worker investment is its own separate factor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare investments not only in dollar value but in type — whether the worker makes similar types of investments as the employer (albeit smaller) that suggest operating independently. Clarifies that unilaterally imposed costs by an employer that merely appear capital-like are not indicative of entrepreneurial investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of permanence of the work relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the degree of permanence or duration of the working relationship between the worker and the potential employer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate aspects such as exclusivity and whether the relationship is ongoing or temporary; permanence or temporariness informs whether a worker is economically dependent. The rule discusses exclusivity in the permanency context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and degree of control
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine the nature and degree of control that the potential employer exercises over the worker and the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control analysis includes scheduling, supervision (including remote supervision), setting a price or rate for goods or services, the employer's retained or reserved rights, and the worker's ability to work for others. The rule allows considering reserved rights and clarifies how control used for compliance with legal obligations should be treated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent to which the work performed is an integral part of the potential employer's business
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the worker's services are an integral part of the potential employer's business (integral factor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This factor looks to whether the work is central or important to the employer's business rather than limiting the inquiry to whether work is part of an 'integrated unit of production.' Integral status can indicate employee-like dependency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skill and initiative
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the level of skill required for the work and the worker's initiative in performing the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule discusses initiative in the context of the skill factor — whether the work requires specialized skill and whether the worker exercises initiative that signifies business independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional factors (other relevant considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow consideration of additional factors beyond the enumerated six where relevant to the economic dependence inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The list of factors is not exhaustive; other circumstances or evidence may be relevant to assessing economic dependence and should be considered in the totality analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of actual practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Give primary weight to the actual practice of the parties (what is done in fact) over what may be contractually or theoretically possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the real-world conduct of the parties rather than labels or contractual terms alone. Note: the rule discusses and adjusts how actual practice and reserved/retained rights are treated to avoid minimizing relevance of reserved rights while still focusing on actual conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of relative investments not solely by dollar value
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing worker and employer investments, focus on whether the worker is making similar types of investments as the employer, not only on dollar amount or size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relative investment comparison should recognize similar kinds of capital/entrepreneurial investments even if smaller in scale; the rule clarifies this in response to comments on the proposed text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unilaterally imposed costs not indicative of entrepreneurial investment
rubrics_metrics.description: Costs unilaterally imposed by a potential employer that appear capital-like should not be treated as evidence of the worker's entrepreneurial investment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the employer requires or imposes costs (e.g., purchasing equipment, paying for training) without reflecting a true entrepreneurial risk or capital stake by the worker, those costs should not be treated as showing independent business status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control implemented for legal compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that employer control implemented for compliance with legal obligations may raise distinct considerations when assessing control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department revised proposed language on control-for-compliance to reduce confusion; the rule clarifies how such compliance-driven controls should be weighed so they are not misread as indicating employee status inappropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of examples and illustrative analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide examples of analyzing economic reality factors to illustrate application of the test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule includes numerous examples demonstrating how each factor (and combinations of factors) may be applied to real-world situations; these examples serve as guidance but do not create rigid rules.
